What the question required: you had to match the element list to a molecule class. The sample contains N and P but no S, so the answer had to fit all three facts, not just one.

What you did: you matched on N and treated S as a clue for a protein. The key evidence was the missing sulfur, which argues against cysteine-rich proteins, and the presence of phosphorus, which proteins do not carry in their backbone.

Why this matters: on elemental-composition questions, every listed element and every absent element is a constraint. A candidate has to account for all of them, and this is worth the full point.

Next move: before choosing, write two columns, "present" and "absent," and check each candidate against both. Then ask which molecule class carries phosphorus as a backbone component.

What the question required: you had to decide which end of a phospholipid faces the water and which end is shielded from it, and recognize that the spontaneous closed bilayer follows from that.

What the student did: choice A reverses the polarity of the two ends. It puts the tails facing water and the heads buried in the middle, which is the opposite of what happens in water.

Why this matters: the phosphate head is hydrophilic, so it stays in contact with water. The nonpolar fatty-acid tails are hydrophobic, so they cluster together in the interior of the bilayer, away from water. Getting this orientation right is the entire point of the question, and it is the single step that earns the point.

Next move: sketch one phospholipid, label the head "hydrophilic" and the tails "hydrophobic," then draw the two layers so each head points outward toward water and each tail points inward toward the other tails. Check each option against that sketch.

text: The question asked you to predict a physical property from bond structure. Fat 1 has only single carbon-carbon bonds, so its chains are straight and pack tightly. Fat 2 has double bonds, which bend the chains and stop them from packing closely. You chose C, which relied only on the shared elements, carbon and hydrogen. Those elements don't determine shape or packing, so the choice doesn't address what the question asked. Earning this point means comparing the bond types. Next move: write one sentence stating how single versus double bonds change chain shape, then use that to predict which fat is more likely to be solid at 4 degrees C.

(1) The question asks you to connect the number of amino acids to the number of water molecules released, which means knowing how many peptide bonds form in a chain.

(2) Choice B counts one water per amino acid. That mistake comes from counting monomers rather than the bonds between them.

(3) Each peptide bond is one condensation step that releases one water. A chain of 50 subunits has only 49 links between neighbors, so the water count tracks bonds, not monomers.

(4) Next move: write the rule as "water released = bonds formed = monomers minus one," then test it on a 3-amino-acid chain by drawing the two bonds and counting the waters.

What the question required: the complementary strand written 5' to 3', which means pairing each base correctly and then reversing the order, since the two strands run antiparallel.

What you did: you paired the bases correctly (A with T, T with A, G with C, C with G), but you kept them in the original left-to-right order. That produces a strand that reads 3' to 5', so the answer fails the direction requirement even though the pairing is right.

Why it matters: the question asks for a specific direction, and the orientation is part of the answer. Base pairing alone earns no credit here.

Next move: after pairing each base, write the new strand, then reverse it so the 5' end is on the left. Check the ends before you finalize: the strand must start with 5' and end with 3'.

text: The question asked you to classify "area code" as a variable type, which means deciding whether the values measure an amount or name a category. Your choice, B (quantitative continuous), treated the codes as measurements that could fall anywhere on a number line. That is the tempting trap: area codes are written as numbers, but they do not measure anything. A code of 415 is not "more" than 212 in any sense that quantity can express, and no value lies between 212 and 213 in a meaningful way. The key test is whether arithmetic on the values means something. It does not here, so the variable is categorical. Your next move: for any numeric-looking variable, ask "does the number measure an amount?" If it only labels a group, classify it as categorical before choosing among answers.

(1) The question asked what a histogram can tell you about one specific value. Bins group scores into ranges, so a histogram can show only how many scores fall in each range, not the exact value of any score.

(2) You chose D, which says a bar chart would show each exact score. That misreads the chart type: bar charts display categorical data, and these scores are quantitative. The claim about exactly 85 cannot be settled from the histogram at all.

(3) This matters because the one point depends on recognizing what a histogram can and cannot display: counts within intervals, not individual values.

(4) Next move: for individual quantitative values, use a dotplot or stemplot. Then reread the question and ask which display shows each exact score.

text:
(1) This question asked you to judge the sample proportion as an estimator: is it biased, and why or why not? That requires reasoning about the sampling distribution, not about one sample.

(2) You chose A, saying the estimator is biased because 0.44 is not 0.50. You judged the estimator by a single result. That is the step that lost the point.

(3) Bias is a property of the long-run center of the sampling distribution. You must check whether the mean of all possible sample proportions equals the true p. One sample that misses the target says nothing about that.

(4) Next move: write the sentence "bias = E(p̂) − p" and ask whether E(p̂) equals p for a random sample. Then reread the answer choices and eliminate any that judge a single sample.

text:
(1) This question asked whether the data support a claim about every plant: "always" makes it a universal statement, so the justification has to address individual plants, not just averages.

(2) Your answer treated the difference in means (59 vs. 55) as proof that every sunny-spot plant is taller than every shaded-spot plant. That moves from an average to individuals, which the data cannot show.

(3) With SDs of about 10 in both groups, the height ranges overlap heavily. Many shaded plants will be taller than many sunny plants, so the claim "always" fails even though the mean is higher.

(4) Next move: for any "always" or "every" claim, ask whether the evidence describes a single value or a summary. Check the spread (SD) before accepting a comparison of means.

text: The question asks which statement best judges whether the data support the claim, so you needed to evaluate the claim against what the survey actually shows. Choice A does not do that. It says the results "prove" a result that holds "always" and "in any future study or population," which goes far past a single survey of the groups described. The means (49 vs. 45) with SDs of about 10 show a difference in averages, not a guaranteed ranking of every student. Statistical evidence from one sample cannot establish something "always" true, and that absolute wording is what makes the choice wrong. Next time, before picking, check whether the answer uses words like "prove," "always," or "any," and ask whether the data can support that strength of claim.

The highest-value missing criterion is the proportional relationship: the response says the rate "goes up" without stating the quantitative link. The requirement is that tripling the area (1,500 to 4,500 μm²) triples the rate (30 to 90). The student wrote "though I didn't check the exact numbers in the table," so that evidence was never used.

Part (b) also needs tightening. The student says the membrane "seems to hold the Q-making part somewhere separate." The stronger explanation is that the membrane keeps breakdown reactions apart from the cytosol where Q is made, and that rupture puts both in the same space so Q is broken down as it forms, leaving 1.5 μmol per gram instead of 12.0.

(d) More internal membrane means more surface for the enzymes to sit on, so more of reaction R can happen at once.

text: Your highest-value missing piece is the calculation in (d). Replace "somehow" with a firm statement: the leftover 9 kJ/mol is released to the surroundings as heat, and none of it is destroyed. Write the subtraction first, then the sentence about heat.
response: (a) The data suggest the blocked step is step 2, because B builds up in the mutant while C and D are missing. (b) Step 3 needs C as its reactant, and since the mutant can't make C, there's nothing for the enzyme to act on, so no D forms. (c) Reaction E is exergonic and releases energy that gets transferred to step 3, which is endergonic and needs energy to go, so the two reactions are linked together and step 3 can happen. (d) I think the leftover energy is just given off somehow, maybe as heat, but I'm not sure how much is left over per mole.

Your highest-value gap is in part (d). You predicted the shrew, which is correct, and wrote "because it's smaller." The question requires you to connect size to surface area-to-volume ratio and then to heat. Say that the shrew's SA:V is higher, so it loses body heat faster per unit of mass, and therefore its metabolism must produce more heat per unit mass to hold body temperature steady. Without the heat-loss link, "smaller" alone does not justify the prediction.

Part (a) also needs a fix: "I'm not totally sure I set up the sphere formulas right" signals doubt, but your 1.5 μm⁻¹ is correct. Trust it and state the setup (SA = 4πr², V = 4/3πr³) so the calculation is visible. For part (b), check cell B's numbers, since you did not verify them.
response: For part (a), I think cell A's SA is 16π μm² and volume is 32π/3 μm³, so dividing gives about 1.5 μm⁻¹, but I'm not totally sure I set up the sphere formulas right. For part (b), I divided cell A's ratio by cell B's, which gives roughly 3 times, though I didn't double-check cell B's numbers. For part (c), cell B has a smaller surface area compared to its volume, so it can't take in nutrients and get rid of waste as quickly as cell A can. For part (d), I'd guess the shrew has the higher metabolic rate because it's smaller, but I didn't really explain the heat loss part clearly.

text:
The highest-value missing piece is in part (c). You wrote that the agency "may be underestimating," but the criterion requires you to say the data give evidence that the true proportion is greater than 0.25. Your reasoning about rarity is right, so state the conclusion in those terms.

Your part (a) and (b) work earned full credit: you counted the 4 simulated samples at or above 20 and divided by 200, then stated the probability in context under the 0.25 assumption.

Next move: rewrite (c) as one sentence: "Because p-value ≈ 0.02 is small, 20 or more app users would be unlikely if p = 0.25, so there is evidence that more than 25% of riders pay with the app."
response: (a) I ran the simulation 200 times and counted how many simulated samples had 20 or more riders paying with the app. I got 2 in one group and 2 in another, so 4 out of 200, which gives a p-value estimate of 4/200 = 0.02. (b) The p-value is the probability that a random sample of 50 riders would have 20 or more who pay with the app, assuming the true proportion is 0.25. (c) The small p-value suggests that getting 20 or more app users would be pretty rare if the true percentage were 25%, so it looks like the agency may be underestimating how many riders use the app. (d) The second analyst's p-value of 0.41 is not small, so that sample didn't give strong evidence against the 25% claim, but that doesn't mean the claim is true. A large p-value just means the result is consistent with 25%, and a single sample can't prove the exact proportion for all riders.

text: Your grader verdicts show all four criteria earned, so the card should confirm that and point to the one place your answer could be sharper. The highest-value move is making your fix fully concrete. You wrote "randomly pick students from the whole school," but the criterion asks you to explain that every student goes on a list and 50 are chosen at random. Name that process directly. Your bias explanation, "people who want to answer are more likely to be the ones who have strong opinions," is correct and already earns the credit, so keep that reasoning. Next time, state the full sampling procedure in one sentence, then tie it back to why it makes the sample representative of the whole student body.
response: The method sounds like a convenience sample since they just asked whoever was eating lunch near them. I think the problem is that people who want to answer are more likely to be the ones who have strong opinions, so it's kind of biased. To fix it, you'd probably want to randomly pick students from the whole school instead of just whoever is around.

text: You earned full credit on every part, so the card should confirm that and point to the one thing worth tightening. Your "either inside or outside" reasoning is correct, but it stops short of connecting the random sampling to that long-run error rate. Next move: add one sentence saying that because of the 95% confidence level, about 5% of intervals built this way would fail to capture p₁ − p₂, so the resident cannot be certain the true difference falls between 0.046 and 0.174. Keep parts (a) through (c) as written, since they meet every criterion.
response: (a) I am 95% confident that the true difference in the proportion of adults who used a public library in the past month, Riverton minus Lakeside, is between 0.046 and 0.174. (b) If we repeated the sampling many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true difference between the two towns. (c) The first board member is supported since the interval does not include 0, so there seems to be a difference. The second claim doesn't seem supported because the interval goes up to only 0.174, which is less than 0.20, so the difference doesn't look like it's more than 20 percentage points. (d) The resident is wrong because the interval came from random samples, and the true difference is a fixed number that is either inside or outside the interval.
